questiontext.text: In risk-based testing, a risk is best described as:

answer.text: A potential problem, characterised by the combination of its likelihood of occurring and its impact if it does

feedback.text: Correct — a risk pairs a likelihood (probability) with an impact (consequence).

answer.text: A defect that has already been found and logged

feedback.text: That is a known defect; a risk is a potential future problem, not a confirmed one.

answer.text: A test case that always fails

feedback.text: A failing test is evidence of a defect, not the definition of a risk.

answer.text: The total number of test cases in the plan

feedback.text: That is a size metric of the suite, unrelated to what a risk is.

generalfeedback.text: A risk is a possible future problem. It is characterised by two dimensions: the likelihood that it occurs and the impact (severity of the consequence) if it does. Risk-based testing uses both dimensions to decide where to focus test effort.

questiontext.text: The likelihood component of a risk refers to:

answer.text: The probability that the failure or defect actually occurs

feedback.text: Correct — likelihood is how probable the problem is.

answer.text: How severe the consequence would be if the problem occurred

feedback.text: That is the impact dimension, not likelihood.

answer.text: The cost of writing the test cases

feedback.text: Test-authoring cost is a project concern, not the likelihood of a risk.

answer.text: The number of testers assigned to the feature

feedback.text: Staffing is unrelated to the probability that a defect occurs.

generalfeedback.text: Likelihood (probability) is one of the two dimensions of risk: how probable it is that a failure or defect will actually happen. The other dimension is impact.

questiontext.text: The impact component of a risk refers to:

answer.text: The severity of the consequence if the failure or defect occurs

feedback.text: Correct — impact is how bad it would be if the problem happened.

answer.text: How probable it is that the defect will occur

feedback.text: That is likelihood, the other dimension of risk.

answer.text: How many test cases exercise the feature

feedback.text: That is a coverage figure, not the impact of a risk.

answer.text: How quickly a fix can be deployed

feedback.text: Deployment speed is a mitigation concern, not the definition of impact.

generalfeedback.text: Impact (severity/consequence) is one of the two dimensions of risk: how damaging the outcome would be if the problem occurred. Combined with likelihood, it gives the risk exposure.

questiontext.text: Risk exposure (the risk level) is normally computed as:

answer.text: likelihood × impact

feedback.text: Correct — combining probability and consequence gives the risk exposure.

answer.text: likelihood + impact

feedback.text: Risk exposure multiplies the two dimensions; it is not their sum.

answer.text: impact − likelihood

feedback.text: Subtracting the dimensions has no standard meaning for risk exposure.

answer.text: likelihood ÷ impact

feedback.text: Dividing the two does not give a risk level; the standard formula multiplies them.

generalfeedback.text: Risk exposure (also called risk level or risk rating) = likelihood × impact. It combines how probable a problem is with how serious it would be, giving a single number used to prioritise testing.

questiontext.text: Risk-based testing is an approach in which:

answer.text: Test effort is allocated in proportion to the assessed risk of each item, testing the highest-risk items first

feedback.text: Correct — risk drives the depth and order of testing.

answer.text: Every feature is tested with exactly the same number of test cases

feedback.text: That is uniform effort; risk-based testing deliberately varies effort by risk.

answer.text: Only features chosen at random are tested

feedback.text: Risk-based testing selects by assessed risk, not at random.

answer.text: Testing stops as soon as the first defect is found

feedback.text: Stopping at the first defect is not risk-based testing; effort is guided by risk levels.

generalfeedback.text: Risk-based testing identifies risks, assesses their likelihood and impact, prioritises them, and allocates more and deeper testing to the highest-risk items — using limited test effort where it matters most.

questiontext.text: A risk matrix (heat map) is:

answer.text: A grid of likelihood against impact used to visualise and rank each item's risk level

feedback.text: Correct — the two axes are likelihood and impact, and cells show the resulting risk level.

answer.text: A table listing every test case and its execution time

feedback.text: That is a test schedule, not a risk matrix.

answer.text: A matrix of code modules against the developers who wrote them

feedback.text: That is an ownership map; a risk matrix plots likelihood against impact.

answer.text: A record of which mutants each test kills

feedback.text: That belongs to mutation testing, not to a risk matrix.

generalfeedback.text: A risk matrix (or heat map) plots likelihood on one axis and impact on the other. Each item lands in a cell; high-likelihood/high-impact items sit in the "red" corner and are tested first.

questiontext.text: Residual risk is:

answer.text: The risk that remains after testing and other mitigation have been carried out

feedback.text: Correct — some risk always remains once mitigation is done.

answer.text: The risk that exists before any testing begins

feedback.text: That is the initial (inherent) risk, not the residual risk.

answer.text: A risk that has been completely eliminated

feedback.text: Residual risk is precisely what is not eliminated; it remains.

answer.text: The risk of running the test suite itself

feedback.text: That is not the standard meaning; residual risk is what is left in the product after mitigation.

generalfeedback.text: Residual risk is the risk that still remains after testing and mitigation. Because testing reduces but never eliminates risk, some residual risk is always present, and stakeholders decide whether it is acceptable to release.

questiontext.text: A product risk (as opposed to a project risk) concerns:

answer.text: The quality of the product itself — that the delivered software may fail to meet needs or contain defects

feedback.text: Correct — product risk is about the software's quality.

answer.text: Schedule slippage caused by a delayed supplier

feedback.text: That is a project risk (schedule/resource), not a product risk.

answer.text: A key team member leaving mid-project

feedback.text: That is a project/staffing risk, not a product-quality risk.

answer.text: The test-management tool licence expiring

feedback.text: That is a project/resource risk, not a product risk.

generalfeedback.text: Product risks relate to the quality of the product — defects, missing functionality, poor performance. Project risks relate to managing the project — schedule, budget, staffing, suppliers. Risk-based testing chiefly targets product risks.

questiontext.text: On a 1–5 scale, an item has likelihood 4 and impact 5. Its risk exposure is:

feedback.text: Correct — 4 × 5 = 20.
That is 4 + 5; risk exposure multiplies the two values.
That concatenates the digits; the exposure is 4 × 5 = 20.
That is 5 − 4; risk exposure is the product, 20.

generalfeedback.text: Risk exposure = likelihood × impact = 4 × 5 = 20.

questiontext.text: An item has likelihood 3 and impact 2. Its risk exposure is:

feedback.text: Correct — 3 × 2 = 6.
That is 3 + 2; risk exposure multiplies the two values.
That is 3 − 2; risk exposure is the product, 6.
That is not 3 × 2; the correct product is 6.

generalfeedback.text: Risk exposure = likelihood × impact = 3 × 2 = 6.

name.text: Testing reduces but does not eliminate risk

questiontext.text: Testing can reduce risk, but it cannot completely eliminate it.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — testing lowers risk (mainly by finding defects and by giving information), but some residual risk always remains.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Testing cannot prove the absence of all defects, so it reduces risk rather than eliminating it; residual risk always remains.

generalfeedback.text: Testing reduces risk by finding defects and by providing information about quality, but no amount of testing eliminates all risk — residual risk always remains. Claiming testing eliminates risk is an overstatement.

questiontext.text: In risk-based testing, when effort must be prioritised, which items are tested first?

answer.text: The items with the highest risk exposure

feedback.text: Correct — highest-risk items get attention first.

answer.text: The items that are quickest to test

feedback.text: Ease of testing may be a tie-breaker, but the primary driver is risk level.

answer.text: The items added most recently to the backlog

feedback.text: Recency is not the ordering criterion; risk exposure is.

answer.text: The items with the lowest impact

feedback.text: Low-impact items are typically deferred, not tested first.

generalfeedback.text: Risk-based testing ranks items by risk exposure (likelihood × impact) and tests the highest-risk items first, so that if time runs out the most important risks have already been addressed.

questiontext.text: Risk is the combination of which two factors?

answer.text: Likelihood and impact

feedback.text: Correct — probability of occurrence and severity of consequence.

answer.text: Cost and schedule

feedback.text: Those are project constraints, not the two dimensions of a risk.

answer.text: Coverage and mutation score

feedback.text: Those are test-adequacy metrics, not the components of risk.

answer.text: Severity and reproducibility

feedback.text: Those describe defects; risk itself combines likelihood and impact.

generalfeedback.text: A risk combines its likelihood (how probable it is) with its impact (how severe the consequence would be). Risk exposure = likelihood × impact captures both.

questiontext.text: On a 1–5 scale, an item has likelihood 5 and impact 5. Its risk exposure is:

feedback.text: Correct — 5 × 5 = 25, the maximum on a 5×5 scale.
That is 5 + 5; risk exposure multiplies the two values.
That concatenates the digits; the exposure is 5 × 5 = 25.
That is 5 − 5; risk exposure is the product, 25.

generalfeedback.text: Risk exposure = likelihood × impact = 5 × 5 = 25 — the highest value on a 5×5 rating scale, marking a top-priority item.

questiontext.text: How should the depth of test design relate to an item's risk level?

answer.text: Higher-risk items get more and deeper tests; lower-risk items get lighter testing

feedback.text: Correct — depth of testing scales with risk.

answer.text: All items get exactly the same depth of testing regardless of risk

feedback.text: That is uniform testing, which ignores risk; risk-based testing varies depth.

answer.text: Lower-risk items get the deepest testing

feedback.text: That inverts the principle; effort should follow the higher risks.

answer.text: Depth of testing depends only on the size of the code, not on risk

feedback.text: Code size may influence effort, but risk-based testing scales depth with risk.

generalfeedback.text: In risk-based testing the depth and rigour of test design scale with risk: high-risk items receive more, and more thorough, tests, while low-risk items receive lighter coverage.

questiontext.text: Three items are rated on a 1–9 scale: A (likelihood 2, impact 9), B (likelihood 5, impact 5), C (likelihood 8, impact 2). Which should be tested first?

answer.text: B — its exposure 25 is the highest

feedback.text: Correct — A = 2×9 = 18, B = 5×5 = 25, C = 8×2 = 16, so B is highest.

answer.text: A — because it has the highest impact

feedback.text: A's exposure is 2×9 = 18, less than B's 25; impact alone does not decide it.

answer.text: C — because it has the highest likelihood

feedback.text: C's exposure is 8×2 = 16, the lowest here; likelihood alone does not decide it.

answer.text: All three are equal, so order does not matter

feedback.text: The exposures 18, 25 and 16 are all different, so B is clearly first.

generalfeedback.text: Compute exposure = likelihood × impact for each: A = 18, B = 25, C = 16. Highest first gives the order B, A, C, so B is tested first. Neither impact nor likelihood alone determines priority — the product does.

name.text: Place an item on the risk matrix

questiontext.text: An item has high likelihood and high impact. Where does it sit on the risk matrix, and how is it treated?

answer.text: In the high-high ("red") corner — it is the highest priority and is tested first

feedback.text: Correct — high likelihood combined with high impact is the top-priority cell.

answer.text: In the low-low ("green") corner — it can safely be deferred

feedback.text: Low-low is the corner for the least risky items; a high-high item is the opposite.

answer.text: Off the matrix, because both values are extreme

feedback.text: Extreme values still land on the matrix — in fact in its most critical cell.

answer.text: In the middle, because the two high values cancel out

feedback.text: High values do not cancel; they compound into the highest exposure.

generalfeedback.text: On a risk matrix, likelihood and impact are the two axes. An item high on both lands in the high-high (red) corner with the greatest risk exposure, making it the first thing to test.

name.text: Why more effort on high-risk items

questiontext.text: Why does risk-based testing allocate more test effort to high-risk items?

answer.text: Because a defect there is both more likely and more damaging, so testing there reduces the most risk per unit of effort

feedback.text: Correct — effort is spent where it buys the greatest reduction in risk.

answer.text: Because high-risk items always contain more lines of code

feedback.text: Risk is about likelihood and impact, not code size; a small module can be high-risk.

answer.text: Because low-risk items cannot contain any defects

feedback.text: Low-risk items can still have defects; they are simply less critical, not defect-free.

answer.text: Because high-risk items are always the easiest to test

feedback.text: Ease of testing is unrelated to risk level; the reason is the greater risk reduction.

generalfeedback.text: With limited resources, testing the highest-risk items first yields the greatest reduction in overall risk exposure. A defect there is more probable and more costly, so effort spent there is more valuable than the same effort on a low-risk item.

questiontext.text: "The only tester who knows the payment module resigns two weeks before release." This is primarily a:

answer.text: Project risk — it concerns staffing/resources, not the product's quality directly

feedback.text: Correct — losing a key person is a project/resource risk.

answer.text: Product risk — it is about a defect in the software

feedback.text: No product defect is described; the issue is a staffing/resource problem.

answer.text: Residual risk — it is what remains after testing

feedback.text: Residual risk is leftover product risk after mitigation, not a staffing event.

answer.text: Neither — staffing is never a risk

feedback.text: Staffing changes are a classic project risk.

generalfeedback.text: Project risks concern the management of the project — schedule, budget, staffing, suppliers. Losing a key tester is a staffing/resource issue, hence a project risk. (It may increase product risk indirectly, but the event itself is a project risk.)

questiontext.text: "The application might compute sales tax incorrectly on some orders." This is primarily a:

answer.text: Product risk — it concerns a possible defect in the delivered software

feedback.text: Correct — a wrong calculation is a quality problem in the product.

answer.text: Project risk — it concerns schedule or staffing

feedback.text: Nothing here is about schedule, budget or staffing; it is about the software's behaviour.

answer.text: Residual risk only, never a product risk

feedback.text: It is a product risk; it may become residual risk if it survives testing, but it is a product risk.

answer.text: Not a risk, because it has not happened yet

feedback.text: A risk is by definition a potential problem that has not yet occurred.

generalfeedback.text: Product risks are about the quality of the software itself. An incorrect tax calculation is a defect in the delivered product, so it is a product risk — exactly the kind of thing risk-based testing targets.

questiontext.text: Items are rated: X (likelihood 3, impact 4), Y (likelihood 6, impact 3), Z (likelihood 2, impact 5). What is the correct test-first ordering (highest risk first)?

answer.text: Y, X, Z
Z, X, Y

feedback.text: That is the reverse; Z's exposure (10) is the lowest, not the highest.

answer.text: X, Y, Z

feedback.text: X's exposure is 12, below Y's 18, so X is not first.

answer.text: Y, Z, X

feedback.text: Z (10) is below X (12), so Z cannot come before X.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: X = 12, Y = 18, Z = 10. Highest first gives Y, X, Z.

questiontext.text: Item P has likelihood 4 and impact 6; item Q has likelihood 7 and impact 3. Which has the higher risk exposure?

answer.text: P, with exposure 24 versus Q's 21
Q, because it has the higher likelihood

feedback.text: Q's exposure is 7×3 = 21, below P's 24; higher likelihood alone does not win.

answer.text: They are equal

feedback.text: 24 and 21 are not equal; P is higher.

answer.text: Q, with exposure 24 versus P's 21

feedback.text: The values are swapped: P = 24 and Q = 21, so P is higher.

generalfeedback.text: P = 4 × 6 = 24 and Q = 7 × 3 = 21, so P has the higher risk exposure despite Q's larger likelihood. The product, not either factor alone, decides priority.

questiontext.text: Item J has likelihood 6 and impact 2; item K has likelihood 4 and impact 3. Compare their risk exposures.

answer.text: They are equal — both have exposure 12

feedback.text: Correct — J = 6×2 = 12 and K = 4×3 = 12.

answer.text: J is higher, because it has the greater likelihood

feedback.text: J = 6×2 = 12, the same as K; a greater likelihood does not by itself raise exposure.

answer.text: K is higher, because it has the greater impact

feedback.text: K = 4×3 = 12, equal to J; a greater impact alone does not raise exposure.

answer.text: They cannot be compared, because their factors differ

feedback.text: They can be compared directly through the product, which is 12 for both.

generalfeedback.text: Risk exposure = likelihood × impact: J = 6×2 = 12 and K = 4×3 = 12, so they tie. Different likelihood/impact combinations can yield the same exposure — which is why prioritisation may then need secondary criteria such as detectability or the severity of the impact.

questiontext.text: Time is short. Three items are rated: Payment (likelihood 5, impact 8), Help page (likelihood 2, impact 3), Login (likelihood 4, impact 7). If one item must be deferred, which is the safest to defer?

answer.text: Help page — its exposure 6 is by far the lowest

feedback.text: Correct — Payment = 40, Login = 28, Help page = 6, so Help page is safest to defer.

answer.text: Payment — because it has the highest impact

feedback.text: Payment's exposure (40) is the highest; deferring it would leave the biggest risk untested.

answer.text: Login — because it is a common feature

feedback.text: Login's exposure (28) is far above the Help page's 6; the Help page is the safer defer.

answer.text: None can be deferred; all are equally risky

feedback.text: The exposures 40, 6 and 28 differ greatly, so the Help page is clearly the least risky.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: Payment = 40, Help page = 6, Login = 28. When time is limited you defer the lowest-risk item, so the Help page is the safest to skip.

name.text: Low likelihood, high impact on the matrix

questiontext.text: A rare but catastrophic event (e.g. permanent loss of all customer data) has low likelihood but very high impact. On the risk matrix it should be:

answer.text: Placed in the high-impact band and still given serious attention, because the consequence is severe

feedback.text: Correct — high impact keeps it important even when likelihood is low.

answer.text: Ignored entirely, because low likelihood means low risk

feedback.text: Low likelihood does not make it negligible; the severe impact keeps its exposure meaningful.

answer.text: Treated as the very lowest priority automatically

feedback.text: A catastrophic impact prevents it from being the lowest priority despite low likelihood.

answer.text: Removed from the matrix because it is unlikely

feedback.text: Unlikely items still belong on the matrix; impact must also be weighed.

generalfeedback.text: Because exposure = likelihood × impact, a very high impact can keep the exposure significant even when likelihood is low. Such rare-but-catastrophic items are placed high on the impact axis and are not dismissed just because they are improbable.

questiontext.text: Even after very thorough risk-based testing, some residual risk normally remains in the product.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — testing reduces risk but cannot eliminate it, so residual risk remains.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No amount of testing removes all risk; residual risk always remains after mitigation.

generalfeedback.text: Testing reduces risk but never drives it to zero — untested combinations, unknown risks and unfixed low-priority defects all leave residual risk. Stakeholders judge whether that residual risk is acceptable for release.

questiontext.text: For a reported defect, how do severity and priority differ?

answer.text: Severity is how serious the defect's effect is; priority is how soon it should be fixed

feedback.text: Correct — severity is about technical impact, priority is about fix urgency.

answer.text: They are two names for exactly the same thing

feedback.text: They are related but distinct: a defect can be high-severity yet low-priority, or vice versa.

answer.text: Severity is set by the customer; priority is set by the compiler

feedback.text: Neither is set by a compiler; both are judgements made by the team/stakeholders.

answer.text: Priority is how severe the defect is; severity is how quickly it recurs

feedback.text: That swaps and distorts the definitions; severity = seriousness, priority = fix urgency.

generalfeedback.text: Severity measures how damaging the defect's effect is (technical impact); priority measures how urgently it should be fixed (business urgency). They often correlate, but a high-severity defect in a rarely used feature may be low-priority, and a low-severity defect on a prominent screen may be high-priority.

questiontext.text: Why should risks be re-assessed periodically during a project rather than rated only once at the start?

answer.text: Because likelihoods and impacts change as the product, information and circumstances evolve

feedback.text: Correct — risk ratings are not static, so priorities must be updated.

answer.text: Because the risk-exposure formula changes over time

feedback.text: The formula (likelihood × impact) stays the same; it is the inputs that change.

answer.text: Because re-assessment guarantees zero residual risk

feedback.text: Re-assessment refines priorities; it does not eliminate residual risk.

answer.text: Because a single early assessment is always perfectly accurate

feedback.text: Early estimates are uncertain; that is exactly why re-assessment is needed.

generalfeedback.text: Risk is dynamic: as code is written, defects are found or fixed, and requirements shift, both likelihood and impact change. Periodic re-assessment keeps the prioritisation aligned with the current state of the project.

questiontext.text: By finding and enabling the fixing of defects, testing most directly reduces which part of a product risk's exposure?

answer.text: The likelihood — fixing found defects lowers the probability that a failure occurs in the field

feedback.text: Correct — testing chiefly attacks the likelihood dimension.

answer.text: The impact — testing changes how damaging a failure would be

feedback.text: The business consequence of a failure is largely fixed by context; testing mainly reduces likelihood.

answer.text: Neither — testing cannot affect risk exposure at all

feedback.text: Testing does reduce exposure, primarily by lowering likelihood.

answer.text: Both are reduced to zero once testing is complete

feedback.text: Exposure is reduced but never to zero; residual risk remains.

generalfeedback.text: Testing finds defects that can then be fixed, lowering the probability (likelihood) that they cause a field failure. The impact of a given failure is usually set by its business context, not by testing. Testing also informs stakeholders, but its direct effect on exposure is mainly through likelihood — and it never reaches zero.

questiontext.text: After test effort has been allocated by risk, what is the correct ongoing activity?

answer.text: Monitor and re-assess the risks, re-prioritising test effort as ratings change

feedback.text: Correct — risk-based testing is an iterative identify–assess–prioritise–monitor loop.

answer.text: Freeze the priorities, since re-assessing wastes effort

feedback.text: Frozen priorities ignore new information; monitoring and re-assessment are essential.

answer.text: Stop all testing once the first high-risk item passes

feedback.text: Passing one item does not address the remaining risks; testing continues by priority.

answer.text: Switch to testing the lowest-risk items exclusively

feedback.text: Effort still follows the highest current risks, not the lowest.

generalfeedback.text: Risk-based testing is a continuous loop: identify risks, assess likelihood and impact, prioritise, allocate effort, then monitor and re-assess. As new defects, information and changes arrive, ratings shift and priorities are updated.

name.text: Prioritise a table of four items

questiontext.text:
Four features are rated on a 1–9 scale:

FeatureLikelihoodImpact
A28
B56
C92
D33

What is the correct test-first ordering (highest risk exposure first)?

answer.text: B, C, A, D

feedback.text: Correct — B = 30, C = 18, A = 16, D = 9.

answer.text: C, B, A, D

feedback.text: C = 9×2 = 18, below B = 30, so C is not first.

answer.text: A, B, C, D

feedback.text: A = 2×8 = 16, below both B (30) and C (18), so A is not first.

answer.text: B, A, C, D

feedback.text: A = 16 is below C = 18, so A must come after C, not before.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: A = 2×8 = 16, B = 5×6 = 30, C = 9×2 = 18, D = 3×3 = 9. Ordering by descending exposure gives B (30), C (18), A (16), D (9).

name.text: Choose two under a time budget

questiontext.text:
There is time to fully test only two of these four items:

ItemLikelihoodImpact
Checkout68
Login47
Search52
Reporting23

Which two should be tested?

answer.text: Checkout and Login

feedback.text: Correct — Checkout = 48 and Login = 28 are the two highest exposures.

answer.text: Checkout and Search

feedback.text: Search = 5×2 = 10 is below Login's 28, so Login should be chosen over Search.

answer.text: Search and Reporting

feedback.text: Those are the two lowest exposures (10 and 6); they are the ones to defer, not test.

answer.text: Login and Search

feedback.text: Checkout (48) is the single highest and must be included; Search (10) should not displace it.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: Checkout = 48, Login = 28, Search = 10, Reporting = 6. With capacity for two, you test the two highest — Checkout and Login — and defer Search and Reporting.

questiontext.text:
Four modules are rated:

ModuleLikelihoodImpact
M135
M244
M329
M462

Order them from highest to lowest risk exposure.

feedback.text: M1 = 3×5 = 15 is not the highest; M3 = 18 is.
M4 = 6×2 = 12 is the lowest, not the highest.
M2 = 16 exceeds M1 = 15, so M2 must come before M1.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: M1 = 15, M2 = 16, M3 = 18, M4 = 12. Descending order is M3 (18), M2 (16), M1 (15), M4 (12) — the close values reward computing each product exactly.

questiontext.text: An item is rated likelihood 8, impact 5 (exposure 40). A mitigation (adding automated input validation plus a targeted test suite) is expected to cut the likelihood to 3, while the impact of a failure is unchanged. What is the new risk exposure?

feedback.text: Correct — new exposure = 3 × 5 = 15.
Mitigation lowers likelihood but does not remove it; residual exposure is 3 × 5 = 15, not 0.
That is the original exposure; the reduced likelihood gives 3 × 5 = 15.
That is likelihood + impact after the change; exposure is the product 3 × 5 = 15.

generalfeedback.text: Mitigation reduces the likelihood from 8 to 3 while impact stays at 5, so the residual exposure is 3 × 5 = 15. Note it drops from 40 to 15 but not to zero — residual risk remains.

name.text: Low likelihood, catastrophic impact warrants testing

questiontext.text: A failure mode has likelihood 1 but impact 10 (exposure 10), while a routine feature has likelihood 3 and impact 3 (exposure 9). Why might the rare-but-catastrophic failure still warrant careful testing?

answer.text: Its exposure (10) is actually higher, and a catastrophic consequence justifies attention even at low likelihood

feedback.text: Correct — 1×10 = 10 exceeds 3×3 = 9, and severe impact matters.

answer.text: Because low likelihood always means low risk, so it can be ignored

feedback.text: Low likelihood does not by itself make risk low; the high impact keeps exposure significant.

answer.text: Because the routine feature has the higher exposure

feedback.text: The routine feature's exposure is 9, below the catastrophic mode's 10.

answer.text: Because likelihood is the only factor that ever matters

feedback.text: Both factors matter; impact can dominate when it is extreme.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: the catastrophic mode is 1×10 = 10, above the routine feature's 3×3 = 9. Beyond the raw number, a catastrophic consequence (e.g. safety or total data loss) often justifies extra testing even when the probability is small, because the cost of being wrong is so high.

questiontext.text: A team claims: "We achieved 100% code coverage, so there is now zero risk of any defect in production." The best critique is:

answer.text: Coverage does not eliminate risk — it does not guarantee correct oracles, cover all data/paths/environments, or address missing requirements, so residual risk remains

feedback.text: Correct — full coverage reduces risk but cannot drive it to zero.

answer.text: Correct — 100% coverage does mean zero remaining risk

feedback.text: This is the misconception; coverage of code executed says nothing about unchecked outputs, missing features, or untried data.

answer.text: Coverage is irrelevant and has no effect on risk at all

feedback.text: Coverage does reduce risk; the error is claiming it removes all of it.

answer.text: The only flaw is that 100% coverage is too expensive

feedback.text: Cost is a separate issue; the key flaw is that even full coverage leaves residual risk.

generalfeedback.text: Executing every line does not verify that outputs were checked correctly, does not exercise every input value, path combination, timing or environment, and cannot reveal a missing requirement. Testing reduces risk but never eliminates it, so claiming zero risk after 100% coverage is an overstatement — residual risk always remains.

questiontext.text: A crash occurs only in an obscure administrative report that one internal user runs once a year. The crash is high severity (it fully stops that function). Why might its fix be assigned low priority?

answer.text: Because it is triggered rarely and affects almost no users, so the business urgency to fix it is low despite the severe local effect

feedback.text: Correct — severity (how bad the effect) can be high while priority (how urgent to fix) is low.

answer.text: Because a crash can never be high severity

feedback.text: A crash that stops a function is genuinely high severity; the point is that priority can still be low.

answer.text: Because severity and priority must always be equal

feedback.text: They frequently diverge; this example is exactly such a case.

answer.text: Because low priority means the defect is not really a defect

feedback.text: It is still a real defect; priority only reflects fix urgency.

generalfeedback.text: Severity measures the technical seriousness of the effect (here, a full crash), while priority reflects how urgently the business needs it fixed. A rarely used, low-exposure feature can carry a high-severity but low-priority defect — the two dimensions are related but distinct.

questiontext.text: The company's name is misspelled in large text on the public home page. Functionally nothing breaks (low severity). Why might this be given high priority?

answer.text: Because it is highly visible and damages the brand, so the urgency to fix it is high even though the functional effect is minor

feedback.text: Correct — high visibility/business impact drives priority up despite low technical severity.

answer.text: Because a cosmetic issue is automatically high severity

feedback.text: It is low severity functionally; the point is that priority is nonetheless high.

answer.text: Because priority is always identical to severity

feedback.text: They diverge here: low severity, high priority.

answer.text: Because low-severity defects are never worth fixing

feedback.text: This one is clearly worth fixing quickly, which is why priority is high.

generalfeedback.text: Severity is low because nothing functionally breaks, but the defect is on the most visible page and harms the brand, so business urgency — priority — is high. This is the mirror image of a high-severity/low-priority defect and shows the two dimensions are independent.

name.text: Residual risk of a deferred item

questiontext.text: Under a deadline, a team fully tests its highest-risk items and deliberately defers a medium-risk item with no testing. On release, what is the correct characterisation?

answer.text: The deferred item contributes to the product's residual risk, which stakeholders should knowingly accept or reject before release

feedback.text: Correct — untested deferred items are exactly residual risk to be acknowledged.

answer.text: There is no residual risk because the highest-risk items were tested

feedback.text: The deferred, untested item still carries risk into production; residual risk is not zero.

answer.text: Deferring an item removes its risk entirely

feedback.text: Deferring testing does not remove the underlying risk; it leaves it unaddressed.

answer.text: The deferred item is now guaranteed defect-free

feedback.text: Not testing something cannot make it defect-free; its risk simply remains unexamined.

generalfeedback.text: Consciously deferring a medium-risk item is a legitimate risk-based decision, but the untested item still carries risk into production. That is residual risk, and good practice is to make it explicit so stakeholders can decide whether it is acceptable to ship.

questiontext.text: Two items tie at exposure 12: item G (likelihood 2, impact 6) and item H (likelihood 6, impact 2). A defect in G would be catastrophic and hard to detect in the field, whereas H's failures are minor and quickly noticed. Which is the more defensible action?

answer.text: Test G more deeply, because with equal exposure the higher-impact, harder-to-detect item deserves the extra rigour

feedback.text: Correct — when exposures tie, secondary factors such as impact severity and detectability break the tie.

answer.text: Test H more deeply, because it has the higher likelihood

feedback.text: Higher likelihood alone does not justify more rigour when the exposures are equal and H's failures are minor and obvious.

answer.text: Skip both, because equal exposure means neither matters

feedback.text: Equal exposure does not mean the risk is negligible; both still matter, and G especially.

answer.text: Test them identically, because the numbers must never be overridden

feedback.text: The exposure number is a starting point; qualitative factors legitimately refine equal-exposure decisions.

generalfeedback.text: Both items have exposure 2×6 = 6×2 = 12, so the product cannot separate them. Risk-based testing then uses secondary criteria: G's catastrophic, hard-to-detect impact makes it the more dangerous of the two, so it warrants deeper testing. This shows the exposure score guides but does not fully determine priority.

questiontext.text: An item initially rated likelihood 2, impact 4 (exposure 8) is later found to sit on a newly discovered critical integration path, raising its likelihood to 7 (impact unchanged). What should happen?

answer.text: Its exposure rises to 28, so it should be re-prioritised upward and given more test effort

feedback.text: Correct — 7 × 4 = 28, a large jump that moves it up the priority list.

answer.text: Nothing changes, because risk ratings are fixed once set

feedback.text: Ratings are not fixed; new information must trigger re-assessment.

answer.text: Its exposure stays 8, because only impact affects exposure

feedback.text: Exposure depends on both factors; a higher likelihood raises it to 7 × 4 = 28.

answer.text: It should be deprioritised, because it was low-risk at the start

feedback.text: The initial rating is superseded; the item is now higher risk, not lower.

generalfeedback.text: Re-assessment recomputes exposure with the updated likelihood: 7 × 4 = 28, up from 8. Because risk is dynamic, the item is moved up the priority order and receives more test effort — illustrating the monitor/re-assess step of risk-based testing.

questiontext.text: Items: R (likelihood 9, impact 2), S (likelihood 3, impact 5), T (likelihood 4, impact 6). A colleague proposes testing in order of likelihood: R, T, S. What is wrong with that plan?

answer.text: Sorting by likelihood alone is wrong; by exposure the correct order is T (24), R (18), S (15)

feedback.text: Correct — exposures are R = 18, S = 15, T = 24, so the correct order is T, R, S, not R, T, S.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; sorting by likelihood always matches sorting by exposure

feedback.text: It does not: T has a lower likelihood than R but a higher exposure (24 vs 18).

answer.text: The plan is right because R has the highest likelihood

feedback.text: Highest likelihood does not mean highest exposure; R's exposure (18) is below T's (24).

answer.text: Exposure should be sorted ascending, so the order is R, S, T

feedback.text: Higher risk is tested first (descending), and R is not the lowest anyway.

generalfeedback.text: Exposure = likelihood × impact: R = 9×2 = 18, S = 3×5 = 15, T = 4×6 = 24. Sorting by exposure (descending) gives T, R, S — different from the likelihood-only order R, T, S. Prioritisation must use the product of both factors, not one factor alone.

questiontext.text: Beyond finding defects, how does executing risk-based tests reduce risk for stakeholders?

answer.text: It provides information that shrinks uncertainty about the true risk level, enabling better-informed release decisions

feedback.text: Correct — test results reduce uncertainty even where no defect is found.

answer.text: It proves the software is completely defect-free

feedback.text: Testing cannot prove the absence of all defects; it reduces uncertainty, not to zero.

answer.text: It permanently sets the risk to zero for every tested item

feedback.text: Residual risk remains even after testing; risk is not driven to zero.

answer.text: It has no value unless a defect is actually found

feedback.text: Even passing tests add value by reducing uncertainty about the risk.

generalfeedback.text: Risk-based testing reduces risk in two ways: by finding defects that can be fixed (lowering likelihood), and by supplying evidence that lowers uncertainty about the actual quality — helping stakeholders judge the residual risk and make informed release decisions. It never eliminates risk entirely.

questiontext.text: A high-exposure item depends on a third-party service that cannot be exercised before release. What is the sound risk-based response?

answer.text: Mitigate by other means (e.g. stubs, contracts, monitoring) and record the remaining untested part as explicit residual risk

feedback.text: Correct — where direct testing is impossible, use alternative mitigation and make the residual risk visible.

answer.text: Declare the item zero-risk because it cannot be tested

feedback.text: Inability to test does not remove risk; if anything the risk is less understood.

answer.text: Ignore it entirely, since untestable items are out of scope

feedback.text: A high-exposure item cannot simply be ignored; it must be mitigated and its residual risk tracked.

answer.text: Assume the third party guarantees it is defect-free

feedback.text: Assuming defect-freeness is unjustified; the residual risk must be acknowledged.

generalfeedback.text: When a high-risk item cannot be tested directly, risk-based testing applies alternative mitigation — service stubs, contract tests, extra monitoring, contingency plans — and explicitly documents whatever risk remains as residual risk so stakeholders can weigh it in the release decision.

questiontext.text: Which sequence best describes the risk-based testing process?

answer.text: Identify risks → assess likelihood and impact → prioritise by exposure → allocate/execute tests → monitor and re-assess

feedback.text: Correct — this is the iterative risk-based testing loop.

answer.text: Write all tests → run them in random order → stop at the first failure

feedback.text: That ignores risk assessment and prioritisation entirely.

answer.text: Assign equal effort to every item → never re-assess

feedback.text: Equal effort with no re-assessment is the opposite of risk-based testing.

answer.text: Fix all defects first → then decide which risks exist

feedback.text: Risks are identified and assessed before, and throughout, testing — not after fixing everything.

generalfeedback.text: Risk-based testing is an iterative loop: identify the risks, assess each one's likelihood and impact, prioritise by risk exposure, allocate and execute test effort accordingly, then monitor and re-assess as the project and its risks evolve.
